Entanglement Breaking Channels

Michael Horodecki Affiliation: Institute of Theoretical Physics and Astrophysics Affiliation: University of Gdańsk, 80-952 Gdańsk, Poland Email: fizmh@univ.gda.pl    Peter W. Shor Affiliation: AT &T Labs Research Affiliation: Florham Park, New Jersey 07922 USA Email: shor@research.att.com    Mary Beth Ruskai Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Tufts University Affiliation: Medford, Massachusetts 02155 USA Email: ruskai@attbi.com
Abstract

This paper studies the class of stochastic maps, or channels, for which (I⊗Φ)​(Γ)(I\otimes\Phi)(\Gamma) is always separable (even for entangled Γ\Gamma). Such maps are called entanglement breaking, and can always be written in the form Φ⁡(ρ)=∑kRk​Tr​Fk​ρ\Phi(\rho)=\sum_{k}R_{k}~{\rm Tr}\,F_{k}\rho where each RkR_{k} is a density matrix and Fk>0F_{k}>0. If, in addition, Φ\Phi is trace-preserving, the {Fk}\{F_{k}\} must form a positive operator valued measure (POVM). Some special classes of these maps are considered and other characterizations given.

Since the set of entanglement-breaking trace-preserving maps is convex, it can be characterized by its extreme points. The only extreme points of the set of completely positive trace preserving maps which are also entanglement breaking are those known as classical quantum or CQ. However, for d≥3d\geq 3, the set of entanglement breaking maps has additional extreme points which are not extreme CQ maps.

1 Introduction

A quantum channel is represented by a stochastic map, i.e., a map which is both completely positive and trace-preserving. We will refer to these as CPT maps. In this paper we consider the special class of quantum channels which can be simulated by a classical channel in the following sense: The sender makes a measurement on the input state ρ\rho, and send the outcome kk via a classical channel to the receiver who then prepares an agreed upon state RkR_{k}. Such channels can be written in the form

Φ⁡(ρ)=∑kRk​Tr​Fk​ρ\displaystyle\Phi(\rho)=\sum_{k}R_{k}\,{\rm Tr}F_{k}\rho (1)

where each RkR_{k} is a density matrix and the {Fk}\{F_{k}\} form a positive operator valued measure POVM. We call this the “Holevo form” because it was introduced by Holevo in [6].

It is also natural consider the class of channels which break entanglement.

Definition 1

A stochastic map Φ\Phi is called entanglement breaking if (I⊗Φ)​(Γ)(I\otimes\Phi)(\Gamma) is always separable, i.e., any entangled density matrix Γ\Gamma is mapped to a separable one.

It is not hard to see that, as shown in the next section, a map is entanglement-breaking if and only if it can be written in the form

Φ⁡(ρ)=∑k|ψk⟩​⟨ψk|​⟨ϕk,ρ​ϕk⟩\displaystyle\Phi(\rho)=\sum_{k}|\psi_{k}\rangle\langle\psi_{k}|\langle\phi_{k},\rho\,\phi_{k}\rangle (2)

in which case it is necessarily completely positive. Furthermore, Φ\Phi is trace-preserving if and only if ∑k|ϕk⟩​⟨ϕk|=I\sum_{k}|\phi_{k}\rangle\langle\phi_{k}|=I, in which case, (2) is a special case of (1). One can show that the converse also holds, so that we have the following result.

Theorem 2

A channel can be written in the form (1) using positive semi-definite operators FkF_{k} if and only if it is entanglement breaking. Such a map is also trace-preserving if and only if the {Fk}\{F_{k}\} form a POVM or, equivalently, ∑k|ϕk⟩​⟨ϕk|=I\sum_{k}|\phi_{k}\rangle\langle\phi_{k}|=I.

The rather straightforward proof will be given in the next section together with some additional equivalences. We will refer to stochastic maps which are both entanglement-breaking and trace-preserving as EBT.

Of course there are stochastic maps which are not of the form (1). In particular, conjugation with a unitary matrix is not EBT. Channels which break entanglement are particularly noisy in some sense, e.g., a qubit map is EBT if the image of the Bloch sphere collapses to a plane or a line. In the opposite direction, we will show that a channel in dd dimensions is not EBT if it can be written using fewer than dd Kraus operators.

Theorem 3

The set of EBT maps is convex.

Although this follows easily from the definition of entanglement breaking, it may be instructive to also show directly that the set of maps of the form (1) is convex. Let Φ\Phi and Φ~\widetilde{\Phi} denote such maps with density matrices {Rj}j=1​…​m\{R_{j}\}_{j=1\ldots m} and {R~k}k=1​…​n\{\widetilde{R}_{k}\}_{k=1\ldots n} and POVM’s {Ej}j=1​…​m\{E_{j}\}_{j=1\ldots m} and {E~k}k=1​…​n\{\widetilde{E}_{k}\}_{k=1\ldots n} respectively. For any α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] the map

[α​Φ+(1−α)​Φ~]​(ρ)=∑jRj​Tr​(α​Ej​ρ)+∑kR~k​Tr​[(1−α)​E~j​ρ]\displaystyle\big[\alpha\Phi+(1-\alpha)\widetilde{\Phi}\big](\rho)=\sum_{j}R_{j}\,{\rm Tr}(\alpha E_{j}\rho)+\sum_{k}\widetilde{R}_{k}\,{\rm Tr}[(1-\alpha)\tilde{E}_{j}\rho]

has the form (1) since {α​E1,α​E2,…​α​Em,(1−α)​E~1,…​(1−α)​E~n}\{\alpha E_{1},\alpha E_{2},\ldots\alpha E_{m},(1-\alpha)\widetilde{E}_{1},\ldots(1-\alpha)\widetilde{E}_{n}\} is also a POVM.

Note that we have used implicitly the idea of generating a new POVM as the convex combination of two POVM’s, In this sense, the set of POVM’s is also convex, and one might expect that the extreme points of the set of entanglement-breaking maps are precisely those with an extreme POVM and pure RkR_{k}. However, this is false; at end of Section 3 of [18], the trine POVM is used to give an example of a qubit channel which is not extreme, despite the fact that the POVM is.

Certain subclasses of EBT maps are particularly important. Holevo called a channel

  • •

    classical-quantum (CQ) if each Fk=|k⟩​⟨k|F_{k}=|k\rangle\langle k| in the POVM is a one-dimensional projection. In this case, (1) reduces to Φ⁡(ρ)=∑kRk​⟨k,ρ​k⟩\Phi(\rho)=\sum_{k}R_{k}~\langle k,\rho k\,\rangle.

  • •

    quantum-classical (QC) if each density matrix Rk=|k⟩​⟨k|R_{k}=|k\rangle\langle k| is a one-dimensional projection and ∑kRk=I\sum_{k}R_{k}=I.

If a CQ map has the property that each density matrix Rk=|ψk⟩​⟨ψk|R_{k}=|\psi_{k}\rangle\langle\psi_{k}| is a pure state, we will call it an extreme CQ map. Note that the pure states |ψk⟩|\psi_{k}\rangle need not be orthonormal, or even linearly independent. We will see in Section 3 that extreme CQ maps are always extreme points of the set of EBT maps, but they are only extreme points for the set of CPT maps if all pairs ⟨ψj,ψk⟩\langle\psi_{j},\psi_{k}\rangle are non-zero.

When all Rk=RR_{k}=R are identical, then Φ\Phi is the maximally noisy map Φ⁡(ρ)=R\Phi(\rho)=R for all ρ\rho. Because it maps all density matrices to the same RR, its image is a single “point” in the set of density matrices and its capacity is zero. A point channel is extreme if and only if its image RR is a pure state. A point channel is a special case of a CQ map; however, because all Rk=RR_{k}=R the sum in (1) can be reduced to a single term with E1=IE_{1}=I. For d>2d>2, one can also consider those CQ maps for which some RkR_{k} are identical; then the POVM can be written as a projective measurement, and the image is a polyhedron.

It is useful to have Kraus operator representations of EBT maps. For Φ\Phi of the form (1), let Ak​m​n=Rk​|m⟩​⟨n|​FkA_{kmn}=\sqrt{R_{k}}\,|m\rangle\langle n|\,\sqrt{F_{k}} where {|m⟩}\{|m\rangle\} and {|n⟩}\{|n\rangle\} are orthonormal bases. Then one easily verifies that

∑k​m​nAk​m​n​ρ​Ak​m​n†=∑kRk​Tr​Fk​ρ\displaystyle\sum_{kmn}A_{kmn}\,\rho\,A_{kmn}^{\dagger}=\sum_{k}R_{k}{\rm Tr}F_{k}\rho (3)

For CQ and QC maps these operators reduce to Ak​m=Rk​|m⟩​⟨k|A_{km}=\sqrt{R_{k}}\,|m\rangle\langle k| and Ak​n=|k⟩​⟨n|​FkA_{kn}=|k\rangle\langle n|\,\sqrt{F_{k}} respectively. Moreover, if all density matrices are pure states Rk=|ψk⟩​⟨ψk|R_{k}=|\psi_{k}\rangle\langle\psi_{k}|, then one can achieve a further reduction to Ak=|ψk⟩​⟨k|A_{k}=|\psi_{k}\rangle\langle k| in the case of CQ maps.

Holevo [6] showed that for EBT maps the Holevo capacity (i.e., the capacity of a quantum channel used for classical communication with product inputs) is additive. This result was extended by King [13] to additivity of the capacity of channels of the form Φ⊗Ω\Phi\otimes\Omega where Φ\Phi is CQ or QC and Ω\Omega is completely arbitrary. Shor [20] then proved the additivity of minimal entropy and Holevo capacity when Φ\Phi is EBT and Ω\Omega arbitrary. Quite recently, King [14] showed that the maximal p-norms of EBT channels are multiplicative, and used this to give another proof of Shor’s additivity results for minimal entropy and Holevo capacity. In a related development, Vidal, Dür and Cirac [22] used Shor’s techniques to prove additivity of the entanglement of formation for a class of mixed states associated with EBT maps.

Because it is important to understand the differences between those channels which break entanglement and those which preserve it, we seek other characterizations of these channels, describe their extreme points, and examine their properties. Results for qubits are given in a related paper [18] which follows. Some analysis of entanglement breaking channels was also independently presented by Verstraete and Verschelde  [21].

2 Equivalent conditions

In this section, we establish a number of equivalent characterizations of EBT maps, some of which were already discussed in the previous section.

Theorem 4

The following are equivalent

  • A)

    Φ\Phi has the Holevo form (1) with FkF_{k} positive semi-definite.

  • B)

    Φ\Phi is entanglement breaking.

  • C)

    (I⊗Φ)​(|β⟩​⟨β|)(I\otimes\Phi)(|\beta\rangle\langle\beta|) is separable for |β⟩=d−1/2∑j|j⟩⊗|j⟩|\beta\rangle=d^{-1/2}\sum_{j}|j\rangle\otimes|j\rangle a maximally entangled state.

  • D)

    Φ\Phi can be written in operator sum form using only Kraus operators of rank one.

  • E)

    Υ∘Φ\Upsilon\circ\Phi is completely positive for all positivity preserving maps Υ\Upsilon.

  • F)

    Φ∘Υ\Phi\circ\Upsilon is completely positive for all positivity preserving maps Υ\Upsilon.

A corresponding equivalence holds for CPT and EBT maps with the additional conditions that {Fk}\{F_{k}\} is a POVM, the Kraus operators AkA_{k} satisfy ∑kAk†​Ak=I\sum_{k}A_{k}^{\dagger}A_{k}=I, and Υ\Upsilon is trace-preserving.

To prove this result, we will make use of the correspondence [2, 12] between maps and states given by Φ↔(I⊗Φ)​(|β⟩​⟨β|)\Phi\leftrightarrow(I\otimes\Phi)(|\beta\rangle\langle\beta|) (Also see [1] in this context.)

Proof: To show that (A) ⇒\Rightarrow (B) note that when Φ\Phi has the form (1),

(I⊗Φ)​(Γ)\displaystyle(I\otimes\Phi)(\Gamma) =\displaystyle= ∑kRk​T2​(Ek​Γ​Ek)\displaystyle\sum_{k}R_{k}~T_{2}\Big(\sqrt{E_{k}}\,\Gamma\sqrt{E_{k}}\Big)
=\displaystyle= ∑kγk​Rk⊗Qk\displaystyle\sum_{k}\gamma_{k}R_{k}\otimes Q_{k}

where T2T_{2} denotes the partial trace, γk=Tr​Ek​Γ\gamma_{k}={\rm Tr}E_{k}\Gamma and Qk=1γl​T2​(Ek​Γ​Ek)Q_{k}=\displaystyle{\frac{1}{\gamma_{l}}\,T_{2}\Big(\sqrt{E_{k}}\,\Gamma\sqrt{E_{k}}\Big)}. Thus, for arbitrary Γ\Gamma, (I⊗Φ)​(Γ)(I\otimes\Phi)(\Gamma) is separable.

The implication (B) ⇒\Rightarrow (C) is trivial. To see that (C) ⇒\Rightarrow (A), observe that since (I⊗Φ)​(|β⟩​⟨β|)(I\otimes\Phi)(|\beta\rangle\langle\beta|) is separable, one can find normalized vectors |vn⟩|v_{n}\rangle and |wn⟩|w_{n}\rangle for which

(I⊗Φ)​(|β⟩​⟨β|)\displaystyle(I\otimes\Phi)(|\beta\rangle\langle\beta|) ≡\displaystyle\equiv 1d​∑j​k|j⟩​⟨k|⊗Φ⁡(|j⟩​⟨k|)\displaystyle\frac{1}{d}\sum_{jk}|j\rangle\langle k|\otimes\Phi(|j\rangle\langle k|) (4)
=\displaystyle= ∑npn​|vn⟩​⟨vn|⊗|wn⟩​⟨wn|\displaystyle\sum_{n}p_{n}|v_{n}\rangle\langle v_{n}|\otimes|w_{n}\rangle\langle w_{n}| (5)

Now let Ω\Omega be the map

Ω⁡(ρ)=d​∑n|wn⟩​⟨wn|​Tr​(ρ​pn​|vn⟩​⟨vn|).\displaystyle\Omega(\rho)=d\sum_{n}|w_{n}\rangle\langle w_{n}|\,{\rm Tr}\,\Big(\rho\,p_{n}|v_{n}\rangle\langle v_{n}|\Big). (6)

Then one easily verifies that

(I⊗Ω)​(|β⟩​⟨β|)\displaystyle(I\otimes\Omega)(|\beta\rangle\langle\beta|) =\displaystyle= ∑j​k​n|j⟩​⟨k|⊗|wn⟩​⟨wn|​pn​⟨j,vn⟩​⟨vn,k⟩\displaystyle\sum_{jkn}|j\rangle\langle k|\otimes|w_{n}\rangle\langle w_{n}|p_{n}\langle j,v_{n}\rangle\langle v_{n},k\rangle
=\displaystyle= ∑npn​|vn⟩​⟨vn|⊗|wn⟩​⟨wn|\displaystyle\sum_{n}p_{n}|v_{n}\rangle\langle v_{n}|\otimes|w_{n}\rangle\langle w_{n}|

where we have used |vn⟩=∑j|j⟩​⟨j,vn⟩|v_{n}\rangle=\sum_{j}|j\rangle\langle j,v_{n}\rangle. Since a map Φ\Phi is uniquely determined by its action on the basis |j⟩​⟨k||j\rangle\langle k|, and hence by the action of (I⊗Φ)(I\otimes\Phi) on |β⟩​⟨β||\beta\rangle\langle\beta|, we can conclude that Φ=Ω\Phi=\Omega. For trace-preserving maps, we also need to verify that {d​pn​|vn⟩​⟨vn|}\{d\,p_{n}|v_{n}\rangle\langle v_{n}|\} is a POVM. Taking the partial trace of (5), and using the fact that Φ\Phi is trace-preserving yields

T2​[(I⊗Φ)​(|β⟩​⟨β|)]\displaystyle T_{2}\Big[(I\otimes\Phi)(|\beta\rangle\langle\beta|)\Big] =\displaystyle= 1d​∑j​k|j⟩​⟨k|⊗Tr⁡(|j⟩​⟨k|)=1d​I\displaystyle\frac{1}{d}\sum_{jk}|j\rangle\langle k|\otimes{\rm Tr}\,(|j\rangle\langle k|)=\frac{1}{d}I
=\displaystyle= ∑npn​|vn⟩​⟨vn|\displaystyle\sum_{n}p_{n}|v_{n}\rangle\langle v_{n}|

which is the desired result. Moreover, we have also shown that (C) ⇒\Rightarrow (D).

To show that (D) ⇒\Rightarrow (A), suppose that Φ⁡(ρ)=∑kAk​ρ​Ak†\Phi(\rho)=\sum_{k}A_{k}\rho A_{k}^{\dagger} with Ak=|wk⟩​⟨uk|A_{k}=|w_{k}\rangle\langle u_{k}|. Then the map Φ\Phi can be written in the form (1) with Rk=|uk⟩​⟨uk|R_{k}=|u_{k}\rangle\langle u_{k}|. Moreover, when ∑kAk†​Ak=I\sum_{k}A_{k}^{\dagger}A_{k}=I, then ∑k|uk⟩​⟨uk|=I\sum_{k}|u_{k}\rangle\langle u_{k}|=I so that Fk=|uk⟩​⟨uk|F_{k}=|u_{k}\rangle\langle u_{k}| defines a POVM.

The equivalence of (E) and (B) follows easily from the fact that a density matrix Γ\Gamma is separable if and only if (I⊗Ω)​(Γ)>0(I\otimes\Omega)(\Gamma)>0 for all positivity preserving maps Ω\Omega [7]. To see that this is equivalent to (F), it suffices to observe that Ω\Omega is positivity preserving if and only if its adjoint Ω^\widehat{\Omega} is and that Φ∘Υ^=Υ^∘Φ^\widehat{\Phi\circ\Upsilon}=\widehat{\Upsilon}\circ\widehat{\Phi}, where the adjoint is taken with respect to the Hilbert Schmidt inner product so that Tr​[Ω^​(A)]†​B=Tr​A†​Ω​(B){\rm Tr}[\widehat{\Omega}(A)]^{\dagger}B={\rm Tr}A^{\dagger}\Omega(B).

It may be interesting to recall that Υ\Upsilon is trace-preserving if and only if Υ^\widehat{\Upsilon} is unital so that the adjoint of a positivity and trace preserving map preserves POVM’s. Thus, when Φ\Phi has the form (1), the map Φ∘Υ\Phi\circ\Upsilon is achieved by replacing EkE_{k} by Υ^​(Ek)\widehat{\Upsilon}(E_{k}).

Conditions (E) and (F) could be weakened slightly since it would suffice to check either for all Υ\Upsilon in some set of entanglement witnesses for the space on which Φ\Phi acts. However, one does not expect to be able to weaken them beyond this. Indeed, [5] and [9] contain examples of a channels which preserve PPT entanglement, but break other types, i.e., the channel output (I⊗Φ)​(Γ)(I\otimes\Phi)(\Gamma) is entangled, yet the partial transpose (I⊗T)(I\otimes T) acting on it always yields a positive semi-definite state (I⊗T∘Φ)​(Γ)≥0(I\otimes T\circ\Phi)(\Gamma)\geq 0.

Alternatively, one could also consider maps which are not EBT, but break particular types of entanglement.

3 Extreme points

We now give some results about the extreme points of the convex set of EBT maps. In this section we will use some additional results from Choi [2] who observed that Φ\Phi is completely positive if and only if (I⊗Φ)​(|β⟩​⟨β|)(I\otimes\Phi)(|\beta\rangle\langle\beta|) is positive semi-definite. When Φ\Phi is written in the operator sum form

Φ⁡(ρ)=∑kAk​ρ​Ak†\displaystyle\Phi(\rho)=\sum_{k}A_{k}\rho A_{k}^{\dagger} (7)

the Kraus operators AkA_{k} can be chosen as the eigenvectors of (I⊗Φ)​(|β⟩​⟨β|)(I\otimes\Phi)(|\beta\rangle\langle\beta|) with strictly positive (i.e., non-zero) eigenvalue. (See Leung [16] for an nice exposition.) Choi [2] also showed that Φ\Phi is extreme in the set of CPT maps if and only if the set {Aj†​Ak}\{A_{j}^{\dagger}A_{k}\} is linearly independent. Since both (7) and this linear independence are preserved when Ai↦∑jui​j​AjA_{i}\mapsto\sum_{j}u_{ij}A_{j}, a sufficient condition for Φ\Phi to be an extreme EBT map is that {Aj†​Ak}\{A_{j}^{\dagger}A_{k}\} is linearly independent for some set of operators {Ak}\{A_{k}\} satisfying (7). Note that the condition that Φ\Phi is also trace-preserving becomes ∑kAk†​Ak=I\sum_{k}A_{k}^{\dagger}A_{k}=I.

Recall that an extreme CQ map is one which can be written in the form

Φ⁡(ρ)=∑k|ψk⟩​⟨ψk|​⟨ek,ρ​ek⟩\displaystyle\Phi(\rho)=\sum_{k}|\psi_{k}\rangle\langle\psi_{k}|\,\langle e_{k},\rho\,e_{k}\,\rangle (8)

with the vectors {ek}\{e_{k}\} orthonormal. We can summarize our results as follows.

Theorem 5
  • A)

    If Φ\Phi is an extreme CQ map, then Φ\Phi is an extreme point in the set of EBT maps.

  • B)

    If Φ\Phi is an extreme CQ map, then Φ\Phi is an extreme point in the set of CPT maps if and only if ⟨ψj,ψk⟩≠0​∀j,k\langle\psi_{j},\psi_{k}\rangle\neq 0~~\forall~j,k when it is written in the form (8).

  • C)

    If Φ\Phi is both in the set of EBT maps and an extreme point of the CPT maps, then Φ\Phi is an extreme CQ map.

  • D)

    When d=2d=2, the extreme points of the set of EBT maps are precisely the extreme CQ maps. When d≥3d\geq 3 there are extreme EBT maps which are not CQ.

Proof: To prove (A) we assume that Φ=a​Φ1+(1−a)​Φ2\Phi=a\Phi_{1}+(1-a)\Phi_{2} with Φ1,Φ2≠Φ\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2}\neq\Phi 0<a<10<a<1 and Φ1,Φ2\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2} both EBT. Both Φ1,Φ2\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2} can be written in the form (2). By combining these, one finds one can write

Φ⁡(ρ)=∑jtj​|ϕj⟩​⟨ϕj|​⟨fj,ρ​fj⟩\displaystyle\Phi(\rho)=\sum_{j}t_{j}|\phi_{j}\rangle\langle\phi_{j}|\,\langle f_{j},\rho f_{j}\rangle (9)

with Φ1,Φ2\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2} having the same form, but different tj≥0t_{j}\geq 0. By assumption, Φ\Phi can be written in the form (8) with |ek⟩|e_{k}\rangle orthonormal so that

Φ⁡(|ek⟩​⟨ek|)=|ψk⟩​⟨ψk|=∑jtj​|⟨ek,fj⟩|2​|ϕj⟩​⟨ϕj|.\displaystyle\Phi(|e_{k}\rangle\langle e_{k}|)=|\psi_{k}\rangle\langle\psi_{k}|=\sum_{j}t_{j}|\langle e_{k},f_{j}\rangle|^{2}\,|\phi_{j}\rangle\langle\phi_{j}|. (10)

Since all tj≥0t_{j}\geq 0, the rank one projection |ψk⟩​⟨ψk||\psi_{k}\rangle\langle\psi_{k}| is a linear combination with non-negative coefficients of the projections |ϕj⟩​⟨ϕj||\phi_{j}\rangle\langle\phi_{j}|. This is possible only if those projections |ϕj⟩​⟨ϕj||\phi_{j}\rangle\langle\phi_{j}| which have non-zero coefficients in (10) are identical to the projection |ψk⟩​⟨ψk||\psi_{k}\rangle\langle\psi_{k}|. Hence, we can conclude that every projection |ϕj⟩​⟨ϕj||\phi_{j}\rangle\langle\phi_{j}| in (9) is equal to one of the projection |ψk⟩​⟨ψk||\psi_{k}\rangle\langle\psi_{k}| in (8). Let us now relabel the projections |ψk′⟩​⟨ψk′||\psi_{k^{\prime}}\rangle\langle\psi_{k^{\prime}}| so that they are all distinct and let Ek′=∑i∈k′|ei⟩​⟨ei|E_{k^{\prime}}=\sum_{i\in k^{\prime}}|e_{i}\rangle\langle e_{i}| where the sum is taken over those eie_{i} for which the associated projection in (8) is |ψk′⟩​⟨ψk′||\psi_{k^{\prime}}\rangle\langle\psi_{k^{\prime}}|. Then {Ek′}\{E_{k^{\prime}}\} gives a partition of II into mutually orthogonal projections, i.e, a von Neumann measurement, and we can write (dropping the ′s for simplicity)

Φ⁡(ρ)=∑k|ψk⟩​⟨ψk|​Tr​Ek​ρ.\displaystyle\Phi(\rho)=\sum_{k}|\psi_{k}\rangle\langle\psi_{k}|\,{\rm Tr}E_{k}\rho. (11)

We can also write

Φ1​(ρ)\displaystyle\Phi_{1}(\rho) =\displaystyle= ∑k|ψk⟩​⟨ψk|​Tr​Fk​ρ\displaystyle\sum_{k}|\psi_{k}\rangle\langle\psi_{k}|\,{\rm Tr}F_{k}\rho (12)
Φ2​(ρ)\displaystyle\Phi_{2}(\rho) =\displaystyle= ∑k|ψk⟩​⟨ψk|​Tr​Gk​ρ\displaystyle\sum_{k}|\psi_{k}\rangle\langle\psi_{k}|\,{\rm Tr}G_{k}\rho (13)

with {Fk}\{F_{k}\} and {Gk}\{G_{k}\} each a POVM. Since the |ψk′⟩​⟨ψk′||\psi_{k^{\prime}}\rangle\langle\psi_{k^{\prime}}| were chosen to be distinct and the Ek′E_{k^{\prime}} orthonormal, it follows that Φ=a​Φ1+(1−a)​Φ2\Phi=a\Phi_{1}+(1-a)\Phi_{2} if and only if Ek=a​Fk+(1−a)​GkE_{k}=aF_{k}+(1-a)G_{k}. Since 0≤Fk,Gk≤I0\leq F_{k},G_{k}\leq I, this is possible only if Fk=Gk=EkF_{k}=G_{k}=E_{k}. But then we have shown that Φ1=Φ2=Φ\Phi_{1}=\Phi_{2}=\Phi, which proves part (A).

To prove (B) note that the Kraus operators can be chosen as Ak=|ψk⟩​⟨vk|A_{k}=|\psi_{k}\rangle\langle v_{k}|. Thus, Aj†​Ak=⟨ψj,ψk⟩​|ek⟩​⟨ej|A_{j}^{\dagger}A_{k}=\langle\psi_{j},\psi_{k}\rangle|e_{k}\rangle\langle e_{j}| which yields a linearly independent set if and only if none of the ψj\psi_{j} are mutually orthogonal. But this is precisely Choi’s condition for the map to be extreme in the set of all CPT maps.

The proof of part (C) requires Lemma 8 which is of interest in its own right. The proof of (D) when d=2d=2 is given in the following paper [18] on qubit EBT maps, while the counter-example establishing (D) for d>3d>3 is given below.

Remark: Recall that a QC map can be written in the form

Φ⁡(ρ)=∑k|ek⟩​⟨ek|​Tr​ρ​Fk\displaystyle\Phi(\rho)=\sum_{k}|e_{k}\rangle\langle e_{k}|\,{\rm Tr}\,\rho F_{k} (14)

with the vectors {ek}\{e_{k}\} orthonormal. Such maps can never be extreme in the set of CPT maps; their Kraus operators always include a subset of the form Ak=|ek⟩​⟨vk|​GkA_{k}=|e_{k}\rangle\langle v_{k}|G_{k} which can not satisfy Choi’s linear independence condition due to the orthogonality of the {ek}\{e_{k}\}. In the case of qubits, QC maps are not even extreme in EBT, unless they are also CQ. However, for d=4d=4, one can have extreme EBT maps which are QC but not CQ.

Example: Let {gk}\{g_{k}\} be orthonormal and consider the POVM consisting of a “trine” on span{g1,g2}\{g_{1},g_{2}\} and the projection on span{g3,g4}\{g_{3},g_{4}\}, i.e.,

E1=23​|g1⟩​⟨g1|,E2=23​|g+⟩​⟨g+|,E3=23​|g+⟩​⟨g+|,E4=|g3⟩​⟨g3|+|g4⟩​⟨g4|E_{1}=\textstyle{\frac{2}{3}}|g_{1}\rangle\langle g_{1}|,~E_{2}=\textstyle{\frac{2}{3}}|g_{+}\rangle\langle g_{+}|,~E_{3}=\textstyle{\frac{2}{3}}|g_{+}\rangle\langle g_{+}|,~E_{4}=|g_{3}\rangle\langle g_{3}|+|g_{4}\rangle\langle g_{4}|

where |g±⟩=12​|g1⟩±32​|g2⟩|g_{\pm}\rangle={\textstyle\frac{1}{2}}|g_{1}\rangle\pm\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}|g_{2}\rangle. Then Φ⁡(ρ)=∑k=14|ek⟩​⟨ek|​Tr​ρ​Ek\Phi(\rho)=\sum_{k=1}^{4}|e_{k}\rangle\langle e_{k}|\,{\rm Tr}\,\rho E_{k} is an extreme EBT map, which is QC, but not CQ.

To see that Φ\Phi is extreme it suffices to observe that it is essentially the direct sum of maps ΦA⊕ΦB\Phi_{A}\oplus\Phi_{B} where ΦA:𝐂2↦𝐂3\Phi_{A}:{\bf C}^{2}\mapsto{\bf C}^{3} with ΦA​(ρ)=∑k=13|ek⟩​⟨ek|​Tr​ρ​Ek\Phi_{A}(\rho)=\sum_{k=1}^{3}|e_{k}\rangle\langle e_{k}|\,{\rm Tr}\,\rho E_{k} and ΦB:𝐂2↦𝐂1\Phi_{B}:{\bf C}^{2}\mapsto{\bf C}^{1} with ΦB​(ρ)=|e4⟩​⟨e4|\Phi_{B}(\rho)=|e_{4}\rangle\langle e_{4}| for all ρ\rho. ΦA\Phi_{A} is extreme because it is the adjoint of an extreme CQ map, and ΦB\Phi_{B} is the only CPT from map 𝐂2{\bf C}^{2} to 𝐂1{\bf C}^{1}. We used the fact that proof of part(A) of Theorem 5 extends easily to map from 𝐂d{\bf C}^{d}to 𝐂d′{\bf C}^{d^{\prime}} with d′<dd^{\prime}<d.

A map which is both CQ and QC projects a density matrix ρ\rho onto its diagonal in a fixed orthonormal basis. One can generalize this to CPT maps which take a density matrix to its projection onto a block-diagonal one. Such maps have the form Φ⁡(ρ)=∑kEk​ρ​Ek\Phi(\rho)=\sum_{k}E_{k}\rho E_{k} where EkE_{k} are the projections in a von Neumann measurement; they are not EBT when at least one of the projections has rank >1>1. The map in the example above is a generalization of CQ in the sense that it is the composition of a block diagonal projection together with an EBT map, and thus could be regarded as “block CQ”. In a similar spirit, one might regard an extreme CQ map for which the ψk\psi_{k} can be split into two mutually orthogonal subsets as “block QC”. With respect to CPT, maps which are both block QC and block CQ could be considered as generalizations of the quasi-extreme points introduced in [19] for stochastic maps on 𝐂2{\bf C}^{2}.

We now give some results about the number of Kraus operators associated with EBT maps.

Theorem 6

If a CPT map Φ\Phi can be written with fewer than dd Kraus operators, then it is not EBT.

Proof: This follows from the fact [2] that Φ\Phi can always be written using at most r≡rank[(I⊗Φ)(|β⟩⟨β|)r\equiv{\rm rank}[(I\otimes\Phi)(|\beta\rangle\langle\beta|) Kraus operators. However, it was shown in [11] that if r<dr<d, then (I⊗Φ)​(|β⟩​⟨β|)(I\otimes\Phi)(|\beta\rangle\langle\beta|) is not separable and, hence, Φ\Phi does not break the entanglement of the state |β⟩​⟨β||\beta\rangle\langle\beta|. Alternatively, one could observe that if r<dr<d, then at least one eigenvalue of (I⊗Φ)​(|β⟩​⟨β|CLOSE(I\otimes\Phi)(|\beta\rangle\langle\beta| is greater than 1/d1/d, while its left reduced density matrix has all eigenvalues equal to 1d1\over d (since Φ\Phi is CPT). However, in Ref. [8] it was shown that if a state is separable, then its the maximal eigenvalue must not exceed the maximal eigenvalue of either of subsystems.    QED

Lemma 7

If Φ\Phi is a CPT map for which rank⁡[(I⊗Φ)​(|β⟩​⟨β|)]=d{\rm rank}[(I\otimes\Phi)(|\beta\rangle\langle\beta|)]=d, then Φ\Phi is EBT if and only if T∘ΦT\circ\Phi is completely positive.

This follows immediately from a (non-trivial) result in [10] which implies that a d2×d2d^{2}\times d^{2} density matrix of rank dd is separable if and only if it has positive partial transpose.

The following lemma is of some interest since one can find examples [4] of separable matrices of rank dd whose decomposition into product pure states requires more than dd products. The additional hypothesis that the reduced density matrix ρA=TrB​ρ\rho_{A}={\rm Tr}_{B}\rho also has rank dd is crucial. The lemma was first proven in [10]. Here we present a simpler proof.

Lemma 8

Let ρ\rho be a density matrix on ℋA⊗ℋB{\cal H}_{A}\otimes{\cal H}_{B}. If ρ\rho is separable, ρ\rho has rank dd, and ρA=TrB​ρ\rho_{A}={\rm Tr}_{B}\rho has rank dd, then ρ\rho can be written as a convex combination of products of pure states using at most dd products.

Proof: Since ρ\rho is separable it can be written in the form

ρ=∑i=1kλi​|ai⟩​⟨ai|⊗|bi⟩​⟨bi|.\displaystyle\rho=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}\,|{a_{i}}\rangle\langle{a_{i}}|\otimes|{b_{i}}\rangle\langle{b_{i}}|. (15)

Assume that k>dk>d and that ρ\rho can not be written in the form (15) using less than kk products. Since ρA\rho_{A} has exactly rank dd, there is no loss of generality in assuming that the vectors above have been chosen so that |a1⟩,|a2⟩,…​|ad⟩|a_{1}\rangle,|a_{2}\rangle,\ldots|a_{d}\rangle are linearly independent. Moreover, since ρ\rho has rank d<kd<k, the first d+1d+1 vectors |ai⟩⊗|bi⟩|a_{i}\rangle\otimes|b_{i}\rangle must be linearly dependent so that one can find αj\alpha_{j} such that

∑j=1d+1αj​|aj⟩⊗|bj⟩=0.\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{d+1}\alpha_{j}\,|a_{j}\rangle\otimes|b_{j}\rangle=0. (16)

Now let {|ek⟩}\{|e_{k}\rangle\} be an orthonormal basis for ℋB{\cal H}_{B}. Then

∑j=1d+1αj​⟨ek,bj⟩​|aj⟩=0​∀k.\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{d+1}\alpha_{j}\langle e_{k},b_{j}\rangle\,|a_{j}\rangle=0~~~\forall~k. (17)

Since the first dd vectors |aj⟩|a_{j}\rangle are linearly independent, there is a vector 𝐱{\bf x} in 𝐂d+1{\bf C}^{d+1} such that ∑jvj​|aj⟩=0\sum_{j}v_{j}|a_{j}\rangle=0 if and only if 𝐯{\bf v} is a multiple of 𝐱{\bf x}. Applying this to the coefficients in (17) one finds that there are numbers νk\nu_{k} such that uj⟨ek,|bj⟩=νkxju_{j}\langle e_{k},|b_{j}\rangle=\nu_{k}x_{j}. Let |ν⟩|\nu\rangle be the vector ∑kνk​|ek⟩\sum_{k}\nu_{k}|e_{k}\rangle. Then αj​|bj⟩=xj​|ν⟩\alpha_{j}|b_{j}\rangle=x_{j}|\nu\rangle. Since |bj⟩|b_{j}\rangle was chosen to have norm 11, it follows that when αj≠0\alpha_{j}\neq 0, |xjαj|=1\left|\frac{x_{j}}{\alpha_{j}}\right|=1 and |bj⟩=ei​θj​|ν⟩|b_{j}\rangle=e^{i\theta_{j}}|\nu\rangle. Thus, one can rewrite (15) as

ρ=∑j:αj≠0λj|aj⟩⟨aj|⊗|bj⟩⟨bj|+∑j:αj=0λj|aj⟩⟨aj|⊗|ν⟩⟨ν|.\displaystyle\rho=\sum_{j:\alpha_{j}\neq 0}\lambda_{j}\,|{a_{j}}\rangle\langle{a_{j}}|\otimes|{b_{j}}\rangle\langle{b_{j}}|+\sum_{j:\alpha_{j}=0}\lambda_{j}\,|{a_{j}}\rangle\langle{a_{j}}|\otimes|{\nu}\rangle\langle{\nu}|. (18)

Suppose that tt of the αj\alpha_{j} are non-zero. Since the vectors {aj⟩:αj≠0}\{a_{j}\rangle:\alpha_{j}\neq 0\} are linearly dependent, the density matrix ρ~A=∑j:αj=0λj|aj⟩⟨aj|\widetilde{\rho}_{A}=\sum_{j:\alpha_{j}=0}\lambda_{j}\,|{a_{j}}\rangle\langle{a_{j}}| has rank strictly <t<t and can be rewritten in the form ρ~A=∑k=1t′λj′​|aj′⟩​⟨aj′|\widetilde{\rho}_{A}=\sum_{k=1}^{t^{\prime}}\lambda_{j}^{\prime}|a_{j}^{\prime}\rangle\langle a_{j}^{\prime}| using only t′<tt^{\prime}<t vectors. Substituting this in (18) gives ρ\rho as linear combination of products using strictly less than kk contradicting the assumption that (15) used the minimum number.

Proof of (C): If Φ\Phi can be written with fewer than dd Kraus operators, it is not entanglement breaking; and if it requires more than dd Kraus operators, it is not extreme. Hence we can assume that rank[(I⊗Φ)(|β⟩⟨β|)=d{\rm rank}[(I\otimes\Phi)(|\beta\rangle\langle\beta|)=d. The result then follows from Lemma 8.

We now show that, for d=3d=3, the set of entanglement breaking maps has extreme points which are not CQ. Moreover, unlike the d=4d=4 example considered earlier, there is no decomposition into orthogonal blocks associated with this map.

Counterexample: Let |0⟩,|1⟩,|2⟩|0\rangle,|1\rangle,|2\rangle be an orthonormal basis for 𝐂3{\bf C}^{3} and consider the following four vectors corresponding to the vertices of a tetrahedron

|v0⟩\displaystyle|v_{0}\rangle =\displaystyle= 13​(+|0⟩+|1⟩+|2⟩)\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\Big(+|0\rangle+|1\rangle+|2\rangle\Big)
|v1⟩\displaystyle|v_{1}\rangle =\displaystyle= 13​(+|0⟩−|1⟩−|2⟩)\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\Big(+|0\rangle-|1\rangle-|2\rangle\Big)
|v2⟩\displaystyle|v_{2}\rangle =\displaystyle= 13​(−|0⟩+|1⟩−|2⟩)\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\Big(-|0\rangle+|1\rangle-|2\rangle\Big)
|v3⟩\displaystyle|v_{3}\rangle =\displaystyle= 13​(−|0⟩−|1⟩+|2⟩)\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\Big(-|0\rangle-|1\rangle+|2\rangle\Big)

and let

Φ⁡(ρ)=34​∑i=03|vi⟩​⟨vi|​Tr​ρ​|vi⟩​⟨vi|\displaystyle\Phi(\rho)=\frac{3}{4}\sum_{i=0}^{3}|v_{i}\rangle\langle v_{i}|\,{\rm Tr}\rho|v_{i}\rangle\langle v_{i}| (19)

We now show that Φ\Phi is an extreme point for the set of entanglement-breaking maps. To see this, first recall that any entanglement breaking map Ψ\Psi can be written as

Ψ⁡(ρ)=∑iαi​|yi⟩​⟨yi|​Tr​ρ​|zi⟩​⟨zi|\displaystyle\Psi(\rho)=\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}|y_{i}\rangle\langle y_{i}|{\rm Tr}\rho|z_{i}\rangle\langle z_{i}| (20)

Let Ψ\Psi be one of the entanglement breaking maps whose convex combination is Φ\Phi, and let |y⟩|y\rangle and |z⟩|z\rangle be |yi⟩|y_{i}\rangle and |zi⟩|z_{i}\rangle for some fixed ii in this above expression for Ψ\Psi. Now, consider the six vectors |wi​j⟩|w_{ij}\rangle for i<ji<j, where these are defined so that ⟨wi​j|vk⟩=0\langle w_{ij}|v_{k}\rangle=0 for k≠i,jk\neq i,j. For example, |w01⟩=12​(|1⟩+|2⟩)|w_{01}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|1\rangle+|2\rangle). Then,

Φ⁡(|wi​j⟩​⟨wi​j|)=12​(|vi⟩​⟨vi|+|vj⟩​⟨vj|)\displaystyle\Phi(|w_{ij}\rangle\langle w_{ij}|)=\frac{1}{2}\left(|v_{i}\rangle\langle v_{i}|+|v_{j}\rangle\langle v_{j}|\right) (21)

so for input |wi​j⟩​⟨wi​j||w_{ij}\rangle\langle w_{ij}|, the output has rank 2 and is orthogonal to wk​lw_{kl}, where i,j,k,li,j,k,l are all distinct. We thus have that for |y⟩|y\rangle and |z⟩|z\rangle,

⟨wi​j|y⟩=0or⟨wk​l|z⟩=0\displaystyle\langle w_{ij}|y\rangle=0\mathrm{\ \ \ or\ \ \ }\langle w_{kl}|z\rangle=0 (22)

where {i,j,k,l}\{i,j,k,l\} is any permutation of {0,1,2,3}\{0,1,2,3\}, as above.

Now, consider |y⟩|y\rangle. Suppose it is orthogonal to two of w01w_{01}, w02w_{02}, and w12w_{12}. Then, we must have |y⟩=|v3⟩|y\rangle=|v_{3}\rangle. This means that |y⟩|y\rangle is not orthogonal to w23w_{23}, w13w_{13} and w03w_{03}, which implies in turn that |z⟩|z\rangle is orthogonal to w01w_{01}, w02w_{02} and w12w_{12}, showing that |z⟩=|v3⟩|z\rangle=|v_{3}\rangle as well.

The other case is when yy is not orthogonal to at least two of the above three vectors w01w_{01}, w02w_{02}, w12w_{12}; we can assume by symmetry that these two are w01w_{01} and w02w_{02}. Then zz is orthogonal to w23w_{23} and w13w_{13}, showing that |z⟩=|v0⟩|z\rangle=|v_{0}\rangle. By the same reasoning as in the last paragraph, we now have that |y⟩=|v0⟩|y\rangle=|v_{0}\rangle as well.

Thus, all the yiy_{i} and ziz_{i} in the above expression for Ψ\Psi must be one of the four vectors vjv_{j}. It follows easily from this that Ψ=Φ\Psi=\Phi. Moreover, we have shown that the Holevo form for Φ\Phi is essentially unique. Hence Φ\Phi can not be written in the form required for it to be a CQ map.   QED

Note that Φ\Phi is not extreme in the set of CPT maps. In fact, it can be represented as a convex combination of CPT maps in several ways. For example, it can be written as the convex combination of the identity map, with weight 13\frac{1}{3}, and the average of the three CP maps that first project the state into one of the three planes {|0⟩,|1⟩}\{|0\rangle,|1\rangle\}, {|0⟩,|2⟩}\{|0\rangle,|2\rangle\}, {|1⟩,|2⟩}\{|1\rangle,|2\rangle\}, and then apply the σx\sigma_{x} operator for that plane interchanging the two basis states, with weight 23\frac{2}{3}. It can also be written as a convex combination of the identity and the four maps corresponding to conjugation with a unitary map which reflects across the plane orthogonal to one of the vectors |vj⟩|v_{j}\rangle.

4 Representations in bases

Let G0=d−1/2IG_{0}=d^{-1/2}I and let G1​…​Gd2−1G_{1}\ldots G_{d^{2}-1} be a basis for the subspace of self-adjoint d×dd\times d matrices with trace zero which is orthonormal in the sense Tr​Gj∗​Gk=δj​k{\rm Tr}G_{j}^{*}G_{k}=\delta_{jk}. Then {Gk}\{G_{k}\}, k=0,1​…​d2−1k=0,1\ldots d^{2}\!-\!1 is an orthonormal basis for the subspace of self-adjoint d×dd\times d matrices and every density matrix can be written in the form

ρ=1d​I+∑j=1d2−1wj​Gj=∑j=0d2−1wj​Gj\displaystyle\rho=\frac{1}{d}I+\sum_{j=1}^{d^{2}-1}w_{j}G_{j}=\sum_{j=0}^{d^{2}-1}w_{j}G_{j} (23)

with wj=Tr​ρ​Gjw_{j}={\rm Tr}\rho G_{j} so that w0=d1/2w_{0}=d^{1/2}. It then follows that

∑j=0d2−1wj2=Tr​ρ2≤Tr​ρ=1​and​∑j=1d2−1wj2≤d−1d.\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{d^{2}-1}w_{j}^{2}={\rm Tr}\rho^{2}\leq{\rm Tr}\rho=1~~{\rm and}~~\sum_{j=1}^{d^{2}-1}w_{j}^{2}\leq\frac{d-1}{d}.

Then any linear (and hence stochastic) map Φ\Phi on the self-adjoint d×dd\times d matrices can be represented as a d2×d2d^{2}\times d^{2} matrix 𝕋{\mathbf{\mathbb{T}}} with elements tj​k=Tr​Gj​Φ​(Gk)t_{jk}={\rm Tr}G_{j}\Phi(G_{k}). Now let Φ\Phi be a Holevo channel with density matrices Rk=∑jwjk​GjR_{k}=\sum_{j}w_{j}^{k}G_{j} and POVM Fk=∑nunk​GnF_{k}=\sum_{n}u_{n}^{k}G_{n} (k=1​…​Nk=1\ldots N) and write ρ=∑ixi​Gi\rho=\sum_{i}x_{i}G_{i}. Then it is straightforward to verify that tj​n=∑kwjk​unkt_{jn}=\sum_{k}w_{j}^{k}u_{n}^{k}. Thus, 𝕋=WT​U{\mathbf{\mathbb{T}}}=W^{T}U where WW and UU are the d2×Nd^{2}\times N matrices with elements wj​k=wjkw_{jk}=w_{j}^{k} and un​k=unku_{nk}=u_{n}^{k} respectively. The condition that {Fk}\{F_{k}\} is a POVM is precisely that the first row of 𝕋{\mathbf{\mathbb{T}}} is (1,0,…,0)(1,0,\ldots,0).

Such representations have been studied in more detail for qubits using the Pauli matrices for GkG_{k}. Recently, several generalizations have been consider for d=3d=3 [15] and higher [3, 17]. Another natural choice of basis has Gj​k=|j⟩​⟨k|G_{jk}=|j\rangle\langle k| for some orthonormal basis |j⟩|j\rangle. In this case some modifications are needed since I=∑kGk​kI=\sum_{k}G_{kk}. For j<kj<k, one could also replace Gj​k,Gk​jG_{jk},G_{kj} by 2−1/2(Gj​k±Gk​j)2^{-1/2}(G_{jk}\pm G_{kj}) which act like σx\sigma_{x} and i​σyi\sigma_{y} for the two-dimensional subspace span{|j⟩,|k⟩}\{|j\rangle,|k\rangle\}. Unfortunately, when d>2d>2, the requirement that RkR_{k} and FkF_{k} are positive semi-definite does not seem easily related to a condition between u0u_{0} and ∑j=1d2−1uj2\sum_{j=1}^{d^{2}-1}u_{j}^{2} in any of these bases. Hence, such representations seem most useful for qubits, as discussed in [18].

For a CQ or QC channel, WW and UU are d2×dd^{2}\times d which implies rank(𝕋{\mathbf{\mathbb{T}}}) ≤d\leq d. Hence the image of a QC or CQ channel lies in a subspace of dim ≤d−1\leq d-1. This raises the question of whether or not a stochastic map for which the image of the set of density matrices lies in a subspace of sufficiently small dimension is always entanglement breaking. (This is true for qubits for which all planar maps are EBT.)

For a basis in which a necessary condition for positive semi-definiteness is ∑i=1d2−1|xi|2≤x02\sum_{i=1}^{d^{2}-1}|x_{i}|^{2}\leq x_{0}^{2}, one can show that EBT implies ∑j=1d2−1|tj​j|≤1\sum_{j=1}^{d^{2}-1}|t_{jj}|\leq 1. For details, see Ref. [18]

In general, a matrix 𝕋{\mathbf{\mathbb{T}}} can be written as a product in many ways. We have shown that 𝕋{\mathbf{\mathbb{T}}} represents an entanglement-breaking map if it can be decomposed into a product 𝕋=WT​U{\mathbf{\mathbb{T}}}=W^{T}U whose elements W,UW,U have very special properties. There is also a correspondence between the matrix 𝕋{\mathbf{\mathbb{T}}} which represents Φ\Phi in a basis in the usual sense and the matrix (I⊗Φ)​(|β⟩​⟨β|)(I\otimes\Phi)(|\beta\rangle\langle\beta|). It would seem that the requirement that (I⊗Φ)​(|β⟩​⟨β|)(I\otimes\Phi)(|\beta\rangle\langle\beta|) is separable is related to the product decomposition of 𝕋{\mathbf{\mathbb{T}}}; however, we have not analyzed this. It may be more amenable to the filtering approach advocated by Verstraete and Verschelde [21].
